--src: Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Trigonometric.Basic
@[simp]
theorem exp_two_pi_mul_I : exp (2 * π * I) = 1 :=
  exp_periodic.eq.trans exp_zero

--src: Mathlib.Data.Complex.Abs
theorem abs_two : Complex.abs 2 = 2 := abs_ofNat 2

--src: Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Trigonometric.Basic
theorem sin_two_pi_sub (x : ℂ) : sin (2 * π - x) = -sin x :=
  sin_neg x ▸ sin_periodic.sub_eq'

--src: Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Trigonometric.Basic
@[simp]
theorem sin_pi_div_two : sin (π / 2) = 1 :=
  calc
    sin (π / 2) = Real.sin (π / 2) := by rw [ofReal_sin]; simp
    _ = 1 := by simp

--src: Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Complex.Arg
lemma arg_exp_mul_I (θ : ℝ) :
    arg (exp (θ * I)) = toIocMod (mul_pos two_pos Real.pi_pos) (-π) θ := by
  convert arg_cos_add_sin_mul_I (θ := toIocMod (mul_pos two_pos Real.pi_pos) (-π) θ) _ using 2
  · rw [← exp_mul_I, eq_sub_of_add_eq <| toIocMod_add_toIocDiv_zsmul _ _ θ, ofReal_sub,
      ofReal_zsmul, ofReal_mul, ofReal_ofNat, exp_mul_I_periodic.sub_zsmul_eq]
  · convert toIocMod_mem_Ioc _ _ _
    ring

--src: Mathlib.NumberTheory.ModularForms.SlashActions
@[simp]
theorem SL_slash (γ : SL(2, ℤ)) : f ∣[k] γ = f ∣[k] (γ : GL(2, ℝ)⁺) :=
  rfl

--src: Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.TwoDim
@[simp]
protected theorem rightAngleRotation (z : ℂ) :
    Complex.orientation.rightAngleRotation z = I * z := by
  apply ext_inner_right ℝ
  intro w
  rw [Orientation.inner_rightAngleRotation_left]
  simp only [Complex.areaForm, Complex.inner, mul_re, mul_im, conj_re, conj_im, map_mul, conj_I,
    neg_re, neg_im, I_re, I_im]
  ring

--src: Mathlib.NumberTheory.ModularForms.QExpansion
theorem periodic_comp_ofComplex [SlashInvariantFormClass F Γ(n) k] :
    Periodic (f ∘ ofComplex) n := by
  intro w
  by_cases hw : 0 < im w
  · have : 0 < im (w + n) := by simp only [add_im, natCast_im, add_zero, hw]
    simp only [comp_apply, ofComplex_apply_of_im_pos this, ofComplex_apply_of_im_pos hw]
    convert SlashInvariantForm.vAdd_width_periodic n k 1 f ⟨w, hw⟩ using 2
    simp only [Int.cast_one, mul_one, UpperHalfPlane.ext_iff, coe_mk_subtype, coe_vadd,
      ofReal_natCast, add_comm]
  · have : im (w + n) ≤ 0 := by simpa only [add_im, natCast_im, add_zero, not_lt] using hw
    simp only [comp_apply, ofComplex_apply_of_im_nonpos this,
      ofComplex_apply_of_im_nonpos (not_lt.mp hw)]

--src: Mathlib.Data.Complex.Exponential
@[simp]
theorem cosh_sq_sub_sinh_sq : cosh x ^ 2 - sinh x ^ 2 = 1 := by
  rw [sq_sub_sq, cosh_add_sinh, cosh_sub_sinh, ← exp_add, add_neg_cancel, exp_zero]

--src: Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Trigonometric.Series
/-- The power series expansion of `Complex.sinh`. -/
lemma hasSum_sinh (z : ℂ) : HasSum (fun n ↦ z ^ (2 * n + 1) / ↑(2 * n + 1)!) (sinh z) := by
  simpa [mul_assoc, sin_mul_I, neg_pow z, pow_add, pow_mul, neg_mul, neg_div]
    using (hasSum_sin' (z * I)).mul_right (-I)

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/-- `Π i : Fin 2, α i` is equivalent to `α 0 × α 1`. See also `finTwoArrowEquiv` for a
non-dependent version and `prodEquivPiFinTwo` for a version with inputs `α β : Type u`. -/
@[simps (config := .asFn)]
def piFinTwoEquiv (α : Fin 2 → Type u) : (∀ i, α i) ≃ α 0 × α 1 where
  toFun f := (f 0, f 1)
  invFun p := Fin.cons p.1 <| Fin.cons p.2 finZeroElim

  right_inv := fun _ => rfl

def RingEquiv.piFinTwo (R : Fin 2 → Type*) [∀ i, Semiring (R i)] :
    (∀ i : Fin 2, R i) ≃+* R 0 × R 1 :=
  { piFinTwoEquiv R with
    toFun := piFinTwoEquiv R
    map_add' := fun _ _ => rfl
    map_mul' := fun _ _ => rfl }

--src: Mathlib.Data.Fin.Tuple.Basic
/-- Equivalence between tuples of length `n + 1` and pairs of an element and a tuple of length `n`
given by separating out the last element of the tuple.
This is `Fin.snoc` as an `Equiv`. -/
@[simps]
def snocEquiv (α : Fin (n + 1) → Type*) : α (last n) × (∀ i, α (castSucc i)) ≃ ∀ i, α i where
  toFun f _ := Fin.snoc f.2 f.1 _
  invFun f := ⟨f _, Fin.init f⟩
  left_inv f := by simp
  right_inv f := by simp

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

  ⟨fun a b =>

If `Estimator.improveUntil a p e` returns `some e'`, then `bound a e'` satisfies `p`.
Otherwise, that value `a` must not satisfy `p`.

theorem Estimator.improveUntil_spec
    (a : Thunk α) (p : α → Bool) [Estimator a ε] [WellFoundedGT (range (bound a : ε → α))] (e : ε) :
    match Estimator.improveUntil a p e with
    | .error _ => ¬ p a.get

  Estimator.improveUntilAux_spec a p e false

--src: Mathlib.NumberTheory.Modular
/-- The function `(c,d) → |cz+d|^2` is proper, that is, preimages of bounded-above sets are finite.
-/
theorem tendsto_normSq_coprime_pair :
    Filter.Tendsto (fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => normSq ((p 0 : ℂ) * z + p 1)) cofinite atTop := by
  -- using this instance rather than the automatic `Function.module` makes unification issues in
  -- `LinearEquiv.isClosedEmbedding_of_injective` less bad later in the proof.
  letI : Module ℝ (Fin 2 → ℝ) := NormedSpace.toModule
  let π₀ : (Fin 2 → ℝ) →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ := LinearMap.proj 0
  let π₁ : (Fin 2 → ℝ) →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ := LinearMap.proj 1
  let f : (Fin 2 → ℝ) →ₗ[ℝ] ℂ := π₀.smulRight (z : ℂ) + π₁.smulRight 1
  have f_def : ⇑f = fun p : Fin 2 → ℝ => (p 0 : ℂ) * ↑z + p 1 := by
    ext1
    dsimp only [π₀, π₁, f, LinearMap.coe_proj, real_smul, LinearMap.coe_smulRight,
      LinearMap.add_apply]
    rw [mul_one]
  have :
    (fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => normSq ((p 0 : ℂ) * ↑z + ↑(p 1))) =
      normSq ∘ f ∘ fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => ((↑) : ℤ → ℝ) ∘ p := by
    ext1
    rw [f_def]
    dsimp only [Function.comp_def]
    rw [ofReal_intCast, ofReal_intCast]
  rw [this]
  have hf : LinearMap.ker f = ⊥ := by
    let g : ℂ →ₗ[ℝ] Fin 2 → ℝ :=
      LinearMap.pi ![imLm, imLm.comp ((z : ℂ) • ((conjAe : ℂ →ₐ[ℝ] ℂ) : ℂ →ₗ[ℝ] ℂ))]
    suffices ((z : ℂ).im⁻¹ • g).comp f = LinearMap.id by exact LinearMap.ker_eq_bot_of_inverse this
    apply LinearMap.ext
    intro c
    have hz : (z : ℂ).im ≠ 0 := z.2.ne'
    rw [LinearMap.comp_apply, LinearMap.smul_apply, LinearMap.id_apply]
    ext i
    dsimp only [Pi.smul_apply, LinearMap.pi_apply, smul_eq_mul]
    fin_cases i
    · show (z : ℂ).im⁻¹ * (f c).im = c 0
      rw [f_def, add_im, im_ofReal_mul, ofReal_im, add_zero, mul_left_comm, inv_mul_cancel₀ hz,
        mul_one]
    · show (z : ℂ).im⁻¹ * ((z : ℂ) * conj (f c)).im = c 1
      rw [f_def, RingHom.map_add, RingHom.map_mul, mul_add, mul_left_comm, mul_conj, conj_ofReal,
        conj_ofReal, ← ofReal_mul, add_im, ofReal_im, zero_add, inv_mul_eq_iff_eq_mul₀ hz]
      simp only [ofReal_im, ofReal_re, mul_im, zero_add, mul_zero]
  have hf' : IsClosedEmbedding f := f.isClosedEmbedding_of_injective hf
  have h₂ : Tendsto (fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => ((↑) : ℤ → ℝ) ∘ p) cofinite (cocompact _) := by
    convert Tendsto.pi_map_coprodᵢ fun _ => Int.tendsto_coe_cofinite
    · rw [coprodᵢ_cofinite]
    · rw [coprodᵢ_cocompact]
  exact tendsto_normSq_cocompact_atTop.comp (hf'.tendsto_cocompact.comp h₂)

/-- Auxiliary lemma showing that for any `k : ℤ` the function `z → 1/(c*z+d)^k` is
differentiable on `{z : ℂ | 0 < z.im}`. -/
lemma div_linear_zpow_differentiableOn (k : ℤ) (a : Fin 2 → ℤ) :
    DifferentiableOn ℂ (fun z : ℂ => (a 0 * z + a 1) ^ (-k)) {z : ℂ | 0 < z.im} := by
  rcases ne_or_eq a 0 with ha | rfl
  · apply DifferentiableOn.zpow
    · fun_prop
    · left
      exact fun z hz ↦ linear_ne_zero _ ⟨z, hz⟩
        ((comp_ne_zero_iff _ Int.cast_injective Int.cast_zero).mpr ha)
  · simp only [Fin.isValue, Pi.zero_apply, Int.cast_zero, zero_mul, add_zero, one_div]
    apply differentiableOn_const

/-- There is no surjection from `α : Type u` into `Type (max u v)`. This theorem
  demonstrates why `Type : Type` would be inconsistent in Lean. -/
theorem not_surjective_Type {α : Type u} (f : α → Type max u v) : ¬Surjective f := by
  intro hf
  let T : Type max u v := Sigma f

  let g : Set T → T := fun s ↦ ⟨U, cast hU.symm s⟩

    intro s t h

      simp only [g, cast_cast, cast_eq] at this
      assumption
    · congr
  exact cantor_injective g hg

/-- The function `(c,d) → |cz+d|^2` is proper, that is, preimages of bounded-above sets are finite.

theorem tendsto_normSq_coprime_pair :
    Filter.Tendsto (fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => normSq ((p 0 : ℂ) * z + p 1)) cofinite atTop := by
  -- using this instance rather than the automatic `Function.module` makes unification issues in
  -- `LinearEquiv.isClosedEmbedding_of_injective` less bad later in the proof.
  letI : Module ℝ (Fin 2 → ℝ) := NormedSpace.toModule
  let π₀ : (Fin 2 → ℝ) →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ := LinearMap.proj 0
  let π₁ : (Fin 2 → ℝ) →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ := LinearMap.proj 1
  let f : (Fin 2 → ℝ) →ₗ[ℝ] ℂ := π₀.smulRight (z : ℂ) + π₁.smulRight 1
  have f_def : ⇑f = fun p : Fin 2 → ℝ => (p 0 : ℂ) * ↑z + p 1 := by
    ext1
    dsimp only [π₀, π₁, f, LinearMap.coe_proj, real_smul, LinearMap.coe_smulRight,
      LinearMap.add_apply]
    rw [mul_one]
  have :
    (fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => normSq ((p 0 : ℂ) * ↑z + ↑(p 1))) =
      normSq ∘ f ∘ fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => ((↑) : ℤ → ℝ) ∘ p := by
    ext1
    rw [f_def]
    dsimp only [Function.comp_def]
    rw [ofReal_intCast, ofReal_intCast]
  rw [this]
  have hf : LinearMap.ker f = ⊥ := by
    let g : ℂ →ₗ[ℝ] Fin 2 → ℝ :=
      LinearMap.pi ![imLm, imLm.comp ((z : ℂ) • ((conjAe : ℂ →ₐ[ℝ] ℂ) : ℂ →ₗ[ℝ] ℂ))]
    suffices ((z : ℂ).im⁻¹ • g).comp f = LinearMap.id by exact LinearMap.ker_eq_bot_of_inverse this
    apply LinearMap.ext
    intro c
    have hz : (z : ℂ).im ≠ 0 := z.2.ne'
    rw [LinearMap.comp_apply, LinearMap.smul_apply, LinearMap.id_apply]
    ext i
    dsimp only [Pi.smul_apply, LinearMap.pi_apply, smul_eq_mul]
    fin_cases i
    · show (z : ℂ).im⁻¹ * (f c).im = c 0
      rw [f_def, add_im, im_ofReal_mul, ofReal_im, add_zero, mul_left_comm, inv_mul_cancel₀ hz,
        mul_one]
    · show (z : ℂ).im⁻¹ * ((z : ℂ) * conj (f c)).im = c 1
      rw [f_def, RingHom.map_add, RingHom.map_mul, mul_add, mul_left_comm, mul_conj, conj_ofReal,
        conj_ofReal, ← ofReal_mul, add_im, ofReal_im, zero_add, inv_mul_eq_iff_eq_mul₀ hz]
      simp only [ofReal_im, ofReal_re, mul_im, zero_add, mul_zero]
  have hf' : IsClosedEmbedding f := f.isClosedEmbedding_of_injective hf
  have h₂ : Tendsto (fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => ((↑) : ℤ → ℝ) ∘ p) cofinite (cocompact _) := by
    convert Tendsto.pi_map_coprodᵢ fun _ => Int.tendsto_coe_cofinite
    · rw [coprodᵢ_cofinite]
    · rw [coprodᵢ_cocompact]
  exact tendsto_normSq_cocompact_atTop.comp (hf'.tendsto_cocompact.comp h₂)

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

  let π₀ : (Fin 2 → ℝ) →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ := LinearMap.proj 0
  let π₁ : (Fin 2 → ℝ) →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ := LinearMap.proj 1
  let f : (Fin 2 → ℝ) →ₗ[ℝ] ℂ := π₀.smulRight (z : ℂ) + π₁.smulRight 1
  have f_def : ⇑f = fun p : Fin 2 → ℝ => (p 0 : ℂ) * ↑z + p 1 := by
    ext1
    dsimp only [π₀, π₁, f, LinearMap.coe_proj, real_smul, LinearMap.coe_smulRight,
      LinearMap.add_apply]
    rw [mul_one]
  have :
    (fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => normSq ((p 0 : ℂ) * ↑z + ↑(p 1))) =
      normSq ∘ f ∘ fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => ((↑) : ℤ → ℝ) ∘ p := by
    ext1
    rw [f_def]
    dsimp only [Function.comp_def]
    rw [ofReal_intCast, ofReal_intCast]
  rw [this]
  have hf : LinearMap.ker f = ⊥ := by
    let g : ℂ →ₗ[ℝ] Fin 2 → ℝ :=
      LinearMap.pi ![imLm, imLm.comp ((z : ℂ) • ((conjAe : ℂ →ₐ[ℝ] ℂ) : ℂ →ₗ[ℝ] ℂ))]
    suffices ((z : ℂ).im⁻¹ • g).comp f = LinearMap.id by exact LinearMap.ker_eq_bot_of_inverse this
    apply LinearMap.ext
    intro c
    have hz : (z : ℂ).im ≠ 0 := z.2.ne'
    rw [LinearMap.comp_apply, LinearMap.smul_apply, LinearMap.id_apply]
    ext i
    dsimp only [Pi.smul_apply, LinearMap.pi_apply, smul_eq_mul]
    fin_cases i
    · show (z : ℂ).im⁻¹ * (f c).im = c 0
      rw [f_def, add_im, im_ofReal_mul, ofReal_im, add_zero, mul_left_comm, inv_mul_cancel₀ hz,
        mul_one]
    · show (z : ℂ).im⁻¹ * ((z : ℂ) * conj (f c)).im = c 1
      rw [f_def, RingHom.map_add, RingHom.map_mul, mul_add, mul_left_comm, mul_conj, conj_ofReal,
        conj_ofReal, ← ofReal_mul, add_im, ofReal_im, zero_add, inv_mul_eq_iff_eq_mul₀ hz]
      simp only [ofReal_im, ofReal_re, mul_im, zero_add, mul_zero]
  have hf' : IsClosedEmbedding f := f.isClosedEmbedding_of_injective hf
  have h₂ : Tendsto (fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => ((↑) : ℤ → ℝ) ∘ p) cofinite (cocompact _) := by
    convert Tendsto.pi_map_coprodᵢ fun _ => Int.tendsto_coe_cofinite
    · rw [coprodᵢ_cofinite]
    · rw [coprodᵢ_cocompact]
  exact tendsto_normSq_cocompact_atTop.comp (hf'.tendsto_cocompact.comp h₂)

      rw [f_def, add_im, im_ofReal_mul, ofReal_im, add_zero, mul_left_comm, inv_mul_cancel₀ hz,
        mul_one]
    · show (z : ℂ).im⁻¹ * ((z : ℂ) * conj (f c)).im = c 1
      rw [f_def, RingHom.map_add, RingHom.map_mul, mul_add, mul_left_comm, mul_conj, conj_ofReal,
        conj_ofReal, ← ofReal_mul, add_im, ofReal_im, zero_add, inv_mul_eq_iff_eq_mul₀ hz]
      simp only [ofReal_im, ofReal_re, mul_im, zero_add, mul_zero]
  have hf' : IsClosedEmbedding f := f.isClosedEmbedding_of_injective hf
  have h₂ : Tendsto (fun p : Fin 2 → ℤ => ((↑) : ℤ → ℝ) ∘ p) cofinite (cocompact _) := by
    convert Tendsto.pi_map_coprodᵢ fun _ => Int.tendsto_coe_cofinite
    · rw [coprodᵢ_cofinite]
    · rw [coprodᵢ_cocompact]
  exact tendsto_normSq_cocompact_atTop.comp (hf'.tendsto_cocompact.comp h₂)

/-- There is no surjection from `α : Type u` into `Type (max u v)`. This theorem
  demonstrates why `Type : Type` would be inconsistent in Lean. -/
theorem not_surjective_Type {α : Type u} (f : α → Type max u v) : ¬Surjective f := by
  intro hf
  let T : Type max u v := Sigma f
  cases hf (Set T) with | intro U hU =>
  let g : Set T → T := fun s ↦ ⟨U, cast hU.symm s⟩
  have hg : Injective g := by
    intro s t h
    suffices cast hU (g s).2 = cast hU (g t).2 by
      simp only [g, cast_cast, cast_eq] at this
      assumption
    · congr
  exact cantor_injective g hg
